thread_title: Ty Mawr, Llandough, Cardiff
subject: Ty Mawr, Llandough, Cardiff
body:
Glamorgan Archives Team,

I am writing to make a targeted archive research enquiry concerning the
DBDT collection and any related Bute, Mountjoy or Western Ground Rents
material held by Glamorgan Archives.

I am investigating the historic title, occupation and parcel
boundaries of *Great
House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough*, particularly evidence concerning a
possible historical division of the farm between land retained by the Bute
Estate and land allegedly sold or transferred to *Daniel Thomas*.

A family witness account describes a specific arrangement under which
approximately ten acres, including the farmhouse, were allegedly sold by
the Bute Estate to Daniel Thomas, while a separate portion of approximately
nine acres remained under the Bute Estate. The account further describes
quarrying on the Thomas-held land and an agreement under which the freehold
would eventually pass to the occupying family when quarrying ceased.

I appreciate that this account requires verification against the original
documentary record. I am therefore seeking to identify the relevant deeds,
agreements, plans and subsequent title documents.
1. Verification of specific DBDT catalogue entries

Please confirm the exact property description, parties and date of the
following catalogue entries, and, if possible, provide a digital copy or
scan of the opening parties clause and any attached or marginal plan:

   -

   *DBDT10/19* – Lease (counterpart), described in the catalogue as
   concerning land and messuages in Bute Street, Cardiff, from trustees of the
   late Marquess of Bute to Mr Daniel Thomas, October 1850.
   -

   *DBDT10/20* – Agreement for a building lease of premises in Bute Town,
   Cardiff, involving the same parties, June 1849.

I understand from the catalogue descriptions that these items concern
Cardiff rather than Llandough. My purpose is to establish whether the *Daniel
Thomas named in these instruments can be identified sufficiently to
determine whether he is the same individual later connected with the
Llandough lime works and land interests*, or whether these are unrelated
transactions involving another person of the same name.

Please also advise whether either document contains information identifying
Daniel Thomas by residence, occupation, estate, trusteeship or other
distinguishing details.
2. Targeted search for a Bute–Daniel Thomas transaction at or near Llandough

Please search the catalogue descriptions and indexes available to Glamorgan
Archives for any deed, conveyance, exchange, sale, transfer, lease,
agreement, plan or related instrument involving:

   - *Daniel Thomas*;
   - *Alfred Thomas*;
   - the *Marquess of Bute*;
   - trustees of the Marquess of Bute;
   - the *Bute Estate*;

and land at or near:

   - *Llandough*;
   - *Great House Farm / Great House / Tŷ Mawr*;
   - adjoining land or parcels that may subsequently have formed part of
   the farm.

I am particularly interested in transactions dating from approximately *1876
to 1878*, but would be grateful for references to earlier or later
documents where they form part of the same chain of title.

In particular, I am seeking evidence capable of confirming or disproving
whether any defined parcel of land was conveyed by the Bute Estate to
Daniel Thomas.
3. Quarrying, lime works and any conditional reversion or transfer

Please identify any relevant records concerning land at Llandough or Great
House Farm that refer to:

   - quarrying;
   - quarries or quarry land;
   - lime works or lime kilns;
   - mineral rights;
   - removal of quarrying machinery;
   - reduction or cessation of rent as land was quarried;
   - termination of quarrying;
   - a future conveyance, reversion, surrender or transfer of a freehold
   interest when quarrying ceased.

The particular issue I am investigating is whether an agreement existed
under which occupation or ownership of a defined parcel was intended to
change when quarrying operations came to an end.
4. Daniel Thomas, Alfred Thomas and the Llandough lime works

Please identify any documents linking *Daniel Thomas*, or his son *Alfred
Thomas (later Lord Pontypridd)*, with:

   - land at Llandough;
   - the Llandough lime works or lime kilns;
   - quarrying operations;
   - Great House Farm or adjoining agricultural land;
   - any freehold or leasehold interest in the area.

I would be particularly interested in estate papers, correspondence,
conveyances, wills, probate-related estate records, rentals, rent books,
abstracts of title and plans that may trace what became of any Daniel
Thomas interest after his death or thereafter.
5. Subsequent title and occupation

Please identify any abstracts of title, estate maps, conveyances,
correspondence, tenancy records or other material that may assist in
establishing:

   1. what happened to any freehold interest held by Daniel Thomas or his
   estate;
   2. whether such an interest was ever conveyed, surrendered or
   transferred back to the Bute Estate or another party;
   3. whether the Bute Estate later reacquired any relevant parcel;
   4. whether later parties, including *Mountjoy Ltd* or *Western Ground
   Rents Ltd*, acquired title to land previously held by Daniel Thomas or
   his successors;
   5. the basis on which later tenancies described as covering the "whole"
   of Great House Farm were granted.

I am also interested in any material linking these title questions with the
occupation of the farm by the *Williams family*.
6. Plans and parcel boundaries

A separate line of research concerns the possibility that historic legal
boundaries passed through or between different parts of the Great House
Farm complex.

Accordingly, please identify any:

   - estate maps;
   - conveyance plans;
   - tenancy plans;
   - quarry plans;
   - large-scale plans;
   - boundary plans;
   - valuation plans;

that show Great House Farm, the farmhouse, garden, stables, outbuildings or
adjoining parcels.

I am particularly interested in documents that could establish whether
different parts of the historic building complex fell within different
legal parcels.

I appreciate that some of these requests may require staff research beyond
a standard enquiry. My immediate priority is to obtain *the relevant
catalogue references and confirmation of what material exists*. If more
detailed searching or document retrieval is necessary, please let me know
the applicable procedure, estimated cost and whether a formal paid research
request would be required.

If relevant documents have been digitised, I would be grateful for details
of the cost of obtaining copies. Otherwise, please advise whether they can
be consulted in person and whether any restrictions or advance ordering
requirements apply.

Thank you for your assistance. The documents identified through this
enquiry may be important to reconstructing the historical chain of title
and occupation of Great House Farm, Llandough from the nineteenth century
onwards.

Yours faithfully,

*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*

thread_title: DBDT79/1 – physical examination of the original
subject: DBDT79/1 – physical examination of the original
body:
Request: physical examination of DBDT79/1. Catalogue entry: Lease (counterpart) of land and premises situate in Pembroke Terrace, Cardiff, from the Marquess of Bute to Mr John Williams, May 1877 [1 parchment, plan in margin].

1. Parties and date – Does the original name the Marquess of Bute and Mr John Williams, and is it dated May 1877?

2. Property description – Exact wording of the land and premises. Does it expressly locate the property in Pembroke Terrace, Cardiff?

3. Llandough / other references – Any mention (body text, plan, schedule, endorsements or annotations) of Llandough, Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Western Ground Rents, or any locality outside Pembroke Terrace?

4. Marginal plan – Does the plan identify the location sufficiently?

5. Further identifying details – Any adjoining owners, plot numbers, parish, street numbers, measurements, previous ownership, rent, consideration, or cross-references to other instruments.

Catalogue wording discrepancy: most other 1877 entries in the series describe the grantor as the “Trustees of the Will of the late Marquess of Bute”. DBDT79/1 is catalogued simply as “from the Marquess of Bute”. From the original, please confirm who executed the lease and in what capacity.

subject: Re: Ty Mawr, Llandough, Cardiff
body:
Louise,

Thanks for your detailed and prompt reply and for the additional
information concerning the Bute Estate records and D696.

I just want to clarify one important point in relation to my original
enquiry, as I think I may have caused a slight misunderstanding about the
particular transaction I am trying to establish.

My principal question is *not whether there are deeds between the Bute
Estate and Alfred Thomas*. The key transaction I am trying to locate and
verify is the *1877 transaction concerning Daniel Thomas and the Bute
Estate*, which I understand from the surviving family evidence to have
concerned a defined portion of Great House Farm, including the farmhouse
and surrounding land. I see an 1877 agreement between both parties, for
that year, but for a different property in Cardiff. I wondered if it was
mis labelled and if you could validify its content, particularly any map
data. So as the integrity of the descriptor of the record is assured or
revisited.

The issue is whether the Bute Estate *conveyed, granted or otherwise dealt
with that defined parcel in favour of Daniel Thomas*, and, crucially, what
the instrument and its plan actually show about the boundaries and the
nature of the interest created. In 1877.

This is important because the present documentary reconstruction I am
preparing treats the 1877 instrument as the potential starting point for
the separate House Plot chain. The working case is that the instrument
dealt with the farmhouse land separately from the eastern
agricultural/quarrying parcel, with provisions connected to quarrying and
the subsequent passing of the house land to the occupying Williams family
when quarrying ceased. That proposition is expressly being treated as a
matter requiring verification against the original instrument and plan,
rather than as an established fact.

I therefore wonder whether the catalogue search could be reconsidered
specifically on the following basis:

*Bute Estate → Daniel Thomas → defined land at Llandough / Great House
Farm, approximately 1876–1878*

including instruments which may not themselves be catalogued under “Great
House Farm” or “Daniel Thomas”, but which might appear under:

   - the name of the property or former field name;
   - the Marquess of Bute or his trustees as grantor;
   - Daniel Thomas as builder, quarryman, lime-burner or occupier;
   - a lease, conveyance, agreement, surrender or counterpart;
   - quarrying or mineral rights;
   - a plan accompanying an instrument;
   - or a transaction recorded in a Bute Estate rental, ledger or estate
   correspondence rather than in the deed catalogue.

I appreciate that your catalogue may simply contain no surviving record of
this transaction. If that is the position, that is useful information in
itself. What I am particularly trying to establish is whether *the 1877
transaction has been positively searched for and not found*, as opposed to
there being no later catalogue entry linking Daniel or Alfred Thomas to the
Bute Estate.
D696 and the later Western Ground Rents material

Thank you also for pointing me towards D696. Please do let me know which
item(s) within D696 contain the *book plans and rental books for Western
Ground Rents Ltd c.1938–1944*, particularly anything relating to Great
House Farm, Llandough or the land occupied by John Williams.

This is potentially very relevant because the documentary issue I am
investigating is whether the later WGR estate corresponded geographically
with the parcel dealt with by the Bute Estate in 1877, or instead with the
separate agricultural/quarrying parcel.
Bute Estate finding aid

I would also be grateful if you could retain my enquiry against the Bute
Estate material being transferred from Cardiff Library. In particular, I
would be interested in any items concerning:

   - Llandough / Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr;
   - Daniel Thomas;
   - the 1870s Bute Estate conveyances or leases;
   - estate plans showing parcel boundaries;
   - quarrying or lime works;
   - rentals distinguishing the farm from the farmhouse/cottages; and
   - subsequent dealings with the relevant parcels.

1910 Land Valuation map

Finally, thank you for identifying DVAL/1/33. If Glamorgan Archives has any
information enabling me to identify the corresponding *1910 valuation map
held by The National Archives*, I would be grateful for the relevant
reference. I am trying to make a targeted request rather than simply asking
The National Archives to search broadly for a Llandough map.

Thank you again for your assistance. The clarification regarding what is
and is not held at Glamorgan Archives is useful, and I appreciate your help
in narrowing down the surviving documentary trail.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*
*Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member*

thread_title: Re: Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough — request for information under FOIA 2000 / EIR 2004
subject: Re: Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough — request for information under FOIA 2000 / EIR 2004
body:
Dr Misra,

Thank you for replying, and for doing so promptly and at a weekend. Good
drills Sir. What an honour. I know you and the Council serve as volunteers,
and I am grateful for the time.

Let me set out plainly what I am asking of the Council, which is narrow. If
you'll allow me?

I am not asking your Council to revisit Mr Egan's answer of 14 June 2026.
He explained that the minute books from 1982 onwards were deposited with
Glamorgan Archives in 2002, and I am pursuing those there.

What I am asking about is what that answer did not cover. Llandough
Community Council is a public authority under Schedule 1, Part II,
paragraph 7(b) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. The Act applies to
the recorded information set out below generally; the Environmental
Information Regulations 2004 apply in addition to any part of it that is
environmental information.

PART ONE — REQUEST FOR RECORDED INFORMATION

1. Whether the Council holds any recorded information created after the
2002 deposit — minutes, correspondence, reports, emails, photographs or
files of any kind — concerning Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) / Church View
Close, the village green in front of St Dochdwy's including registered
green VG 41, or the roadside verge by the churchyard wall.

2. Whether the Council holds any photographs, postcards or images of the
farm, the barn, the green or the church surroundings, of any date.

3. Whether the Council holds any recorded information showing what, if
anything, transferred to it from Penarth Town Council at the 1982
reorganisation, and any recorded information identifying where the pre-1982
Llandough community records were deposited.

If the answer to any of these is that no such information is held, I would
be content with a short statement to that effect — but I do need it stated.
Section 1(1)(a) of the Act requires the Council to confirm or deny whether
the information is held.

Section 10 (and regulation 5 of the EIR) allows twenty working days from
receipt, which on my request of 20 September 2026 I calculate as 16 October
2026.

If the Council is refusing, section 17 (and regulation 14) requires a
written refusal notice identifying the exemption or exception relied on;
section 17(7) requires the Council to give particulars of any complaints
procedure it operates, or to state that it has none, and to notify me of my
right to apply to the Information Commissioner; and regulation 11 gives a
right to an internal review of any refusal under the EIR.

"We have nothing more to add" does not meet those requirements. If the
period passes without a compliant response I will have no option but to
complain to the Information Commissioner.

PART TWO — MATTERS FOR THE COUNCIL'S DISCRETION

These are not part of the request above and carry no deadline. They are
simply things I would be grateful for.

A. I am not asking for the name or contact details of any individual. I am
asking whether the Council would be willing to pass my details to any
former member, former clerk or long-standing resident who might remember
the village between the 1950s and the 1990s, leaving it entirely to them
whether to contact me. I appreciate the Council may have data protection or
administrative reasons for declining, and I would not press it.

B. Whether the Council would be willing to table this correspondence at a
meeting and minute it. I am content for it to be tabled in full.

C. Whether the Council would consider, in due course, whether an
interpretation board or a plaque near the green would be appropriate. The
excavation on the land beneath Church View Close recorded 1,026 burials,
described in the published report as by far the largest early medieval
burial population so far recovered from Wales, above a Roman villa and an
Iron Age roundhouse. That history belongs to Llandough as much as to my
family, and there is nothing on the ground that records it. I would be glad
to give the Council or the community a short talk on the documentary
record, without charge, if that would be useful.

I should be grateful for a response to items 1 to 3 by 16 October 2026.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/ Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

subject: Freedom of Information Request: Reference CAS-347296-M0V4Y1
attachments: Item 01 - Release Schedule_On Discovery_Redacted.csv; Item 02 - Release Schedule_High Level Delivery Schedule_Redacted.csv; Item 03 - Collect 27 Series 11_Manifest_Redacted.csv
body:
I can confirm that The National Archives holds some information relevant to your request.

The initial response from our records enquiries team looked for the four terms (“Great House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or “Cedfin”) within the PRO and RW series and did not find any relevant information. We have now tried those terms and the further twelve terms that you have specified in a wider catalogue search.

The crux of your query is local land ownership dispute in Glamorgan and the demolition of some buildings by a private company; generally speaking, these are not matters dealt with by central government and we would not expect to see anything within our collections. As such, there would have been no records to transfer. The exception is the court case relating to BP properties, which generated some papers.

There are likely to be records of the farm in the 1940s as part of the National Farm Survey series but these cannot all currently be searched online by farm. There are Agricultural Executive Committee minutes and papers for Glamorgan; but again, these cannot be searched online by name of farm and we are unable to conduct this research without charging a fee.

1. Western Ground Rents Ltd — Relevant information not found.
2. BP Pension Trust Ltd — Relevant information not found.
3. BP Properties Ltd — Judicial Papers A-C 1-63 (House of Lords as court of appeal).
4. Mountjoy Ltd — Relevant information not found.
5. Proceedings in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 — Judicial Papers A-C 1-63 (House of Lords as court of appeal).
6. 1982–1983 registration and associated government or administrative records — Relevant information not found.
7. 1980–1988 public campaign and governmental correspondence — Relevant information not found.
8. 1988 eviction and demolition — Relevant information not found.
9. Cadw or central-government communications concerning the property — Relevant information not found.
10. European Commission of Human Rights Application 14464/88 — Relevant information not found.
11. Records concerning transfer, destruction or disposal — Judicial Papers A-C 1-63, YHL/PO/JO/10/11/2536. The series that this record formed part of were released on our catalogue on Discovery on 20th May 2026. This is an open record and available to the public at Kew. TNA holds transfer paperwork for YHL/PO/JO/10/11/2536 (Items 01–03 attached, with out-of-scope redactions).
12. HMC9/311 — Manorial Documents Register returns for Glamorgan. The Manorial Documents Register can now be searched online by manor or parish. Individual farm names are not listed in the titles, and the records are not held at TNA.

This is the limit of what our catalogue metadata and corporate records allow us to confirm.

Ref: 2026/4097

Dear Sion Buckler,

Thank you for your email received into our enquiries system 8th September. Please find below answers to your questions in turn. Please note that prices quoted are without VAT based on the fact that you are in Patagonia.

**26 May 2026 (2026/2370)**
1. 1974 demolition petition, Llandough juxta Penarth — ref or not held.

**29 May 2026 FOIA/EIR (2026/2372)**

2. Williams/Buckler as owners, tenants, or reporters of the 1880 floor discovery.
One source of information about ownership would be rate books. UC/73/1 is a rate book for 1882 – this is the nearest we have to 1880. A search of this (and later volumes UC/73/1-5 covers 1882-1902 and then UDPE/T/30 and UDPE/T/32 cover dates after 1900) could be undertaken by staff on your behalf at a charge of £50 which would include copies of relevant entries.

3. Gaps / missing volumes / withdrawals 1950–1989.
We have never had a full set of records that would show the full tenancy/ownership history of Great House / Ty Mawr Farm. With all historical research of this nature, it is necessary to piece together information from surviving records that have been deposited with us. There are not any records that have been withdrawn from our collections that would have provided additional information to this search for the period 1950-1989.

4. Why the fabric was not scheduled before 1988 (or “Cadw holds this; we hold nothing”).
Not held in our collections – suggest contacting Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales.

5. Internal preservation assessments.
As above - suggest contacting Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales.

6. Planning files for this acreage / demolition / Church View Close — file refs, not class names.
We do not hold planning files (it is possible some files may still be held by the Vale of Glamorgan Council Planning Department), but we do hold copies of the Planning Committee minutes and reports. Mary Buckler started looking at the Planning Committee minutes and reports on her last visit to the searchroom on 13th August. The document references to start with for these would be DCVG/C/4/36/76-77 and DCVG/C/4/36/94 these are for the planning applications 1989/01396/OUT and 1992/00671/RES. It is possible that the minutes may make reference to any earlier applications or discussions. A search of these records and anything else that they lead to could be carried out by staff at a charge of £50 to include copies of any relevant pages found.

7. When the known archaeology was raised in planning.
If any record of this is in our collections it would appear in the Planning Committee records described above in point 6.

8. EIAs / HER / developer briefs 1980–1990.
The HER for Wales is searchable via the Heneb website: Historic Environment Records (HER) - Heneb. You could also contact the Glamorgan Gwent Archaeological Trust to see if they have any relevant information.

**27 July / 5 August 2026 (2026/3309)**
9. DB/E/1–2 Stewart survey / Cedfin.
This was consulted and photographed by Mary Buckler in our public searchroom. If you would like to receive copies of the pages relating to Ty Mawr this would be two images (one from DB/E/1 the survey and one from DB/E/2 the terrier). Total cost £17 (£13 for the first image in the order and £4 for the next image).

10. Lambert Williams–Bute agreements 1818–1835 (not the D160 maps already seen).
Not held. Possibly at the National Library of Wales?

11. Material related to NLW D219.
Not held – this is a National Library of Wales reference: Llandough manorial leases and agreements, - National Library of Wales Archives and Manuscripts You should contact the NLW for access or copies.

12. D153/4–8 1876 limeworks severance — not seen.
Not held – this is a National Library of Wales reference: Deeds relating to premises in p. Llandough, co. Glam., comprising a dwelling house adjoining the churchyard, 1811 (D153/1-2), land (19 ..., - National Library of Wales Archives and Manuscripts. You should contact the NLW for access or copies.

13. DXJF/64/27–32 full sketch bundle — notes seen; confirm sketches and refs.
We believe that the specific references within the bundle 27-32 that would be of interest to you are items DXJF/64/30-31: sketch of former layout of part of village of Llandough-juxta-Penarth by Mrs. Nancy Buckler of great house farm, Llandough, with notes c1950 [1 card, 1 paper]. Is that what you have already seen? Other items in the bundle do not relate to Llandough.

14. DCOWHS on Buckler of Penarth (not DCO/WHS/2).
DCOWHS/2 is the only part of the DCOWHS (Cowbridge and District Local History Society) that relates to Buckler of Penarth. No other records held.

15. Exact ref of the Nov 1877 counterpart already photographed; separate July 1877 counterpart?
I think the items described below have been discussed previously – are these what you are seeking? Please confirm and we can provide a quote for producing copies if required.

Document reference

  * DBDT/1/3
Title

  * Adamsdown Square leases from the trustees of the will of the late Marquess of Bute. Lease to Mr John Williams
Level of description

  * Item
Date

  * Jul 1877
Extent

  * 1 parchment; plan in margin

Document reference

  * DBDT/18/1
Title

  * Lease (counterpart) of land and premises situate in Clyde Street, Roath from the trustees of the Will of the late Marquess of Bute to Mr John Williams
Level of description

  * Item
Date

  * Nov 1877
Extent

  * 1 parchment; plan in margin

16. Cardiff RDC records for this farm.
No records found. The area was not covered by Cardiff Rural District Council but rather Penarth Urban District Council.

17. DRA 418–420 / DRA 5/31 if this site.
Neither of these are complete document references from our collection. Perhaps you could check these references or let us know what you think they should be and we will be happy to search our catalogue.

18. UDPE/S/1/68.
This was viewed by Mary Buckler on 6th August and is a set of plans for a pair of semi-detached houses on the road between Dinas Powys and Llandough. If you would like copies of these plans 5 images will be required at a charge of £20.

19. Penarth estate/tithe/OS/boundary plans of the house plot (not Cowbridge 1924/38).
The relevant estate map would be the Bute Estate survey which is referred to in point 9 above. You can view the tithe map online here: Tithe Maps of Wales along with the accompanying apportionment: Tithe Maps of Wales. Many historic Ordnance Survey maps can also be viewed online, for example through the National Library of Scotland website: Map Finder - with Outlines - National Library of Scotland.

20. WGR / Mountjoy / BP Pension Trust / BP Properties papers.
The only relevant papers we have are those mentioned in point 5.4 in my email of 7th September: collection reference D696 – book of plans and rental books for land owned by Western Ground Rents Ltd c1938-1944. A search of these records could be carried out on your behalf at a charge of £50.

21. Associated bundles stored separately.
All catalogues have been searched for your enquiry.

22. Uncatalogued / recent deposits 1875–1988.
A search of our accessions database, which records all records received into our collection even if they haven’t yet been catalogued, has not revealed any additional records.

23. Photography for copies to Patagonia — rules.
Please find attached the digital photography order form which applies wherever you are based. As mentioned above, prices quoted do not include VAT due to your location. You need to sign and agree to the declaration on the order form.

We hope that this information is of use to you. We will respond to other outstanding emails in due course.

thread_title: RE: Epexio contact us form submission
subject: Re: Epexio contact us form submission
body:
Louise,

Thank you again for your very detailed response under reference 2026/4097.

You have been extremely helpful throughout this research, and I am very
conscious of that. I do travel back and forth to the UK and will visit
Leckwith in person, where I look forward to meeting you and the team and
thanking you personally.

I wanted to reply because I think I can now explain more precisely what I
am trying to establish from the records.

I am trying to reconstruct what happened historically which led my late
grandmother and father, over many decades, to continue asserting that our
family owned the land at Great House Farm, while that position was
repeatedly contested and ultimately possession was awarded to BP in *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler*.

What has caused me to revisit the documentary history is that the later
position is not as straightforward as I had previously assumed. Land
Registry has now told me that its position is not that it determined that
my family did not own the land; but it insists that no registration mistake
has been identified, which is what the MP forwarded me (they're fobbing him
off too).

Land registry will wake up to this soon I'm sure. Or I'm wrong and I need
to wake up. But I am a military warfare professional, and while I make
mistakes, or AI makes mistakes on my behalf, I have no issue holding my
hands up. I'm just trying to understand what happened to us and our home
and our land as children in the 80's, and why it all happened.

At the same time, I have so far found no convincing documentary evidence of
my family paying rent for the particular parcel which we occupied and
claimed as our own after the quarrying arrangement appears to have come to
an end.

I have therefore had one of my AI agents published my current
reconstruction, including the documentary sources behind it, here:

Great House Farm research 

I am not asking you to accept that reconstruction. It's clearly hit and
miss as an early technology. I am asking for your help in testing it
against the records held by Glamorgan Archives.
The central question

My present understanding is that what had originally been treated as one
agricultural holding can, when the surviving documents are examined
chronologically, be distinguished into two areas.

For simplicity, I have called them *Parcel A* and *Parcel B*:

   - *Parcel A* — the farmhouse, house plot, garden and associated land
   north/west of St Dochdwy's Church, occupied by my family; and
   - *Parcel B* — the agricultural land to the east which was subject to
   the agricultural tenancy and subsequently associated with Western Ground
   Rents.

I appreciate that “Parcel A” and “Parcel B” are my labels, not historical
descriptions appearing in the documents. But they aren't entirely just my
labels, parcel B is clearly what is in the 1939 map, which you hold, which
the council clerk for Llandough directed me to earlier this year, on his
day of retirement.

Also in 1983 two parcels were merged at the land registry, by BP. Which
confirms two parcels. I have purchased all those records avaliable and the
maps do confirm what I suspect.

The important question is whether the *underlying documents themselves
support the physical distinction*.

My working reconstruction is that the 1877 Daniel Thomas/Williams
arrangements ultimately resulted in my family acquiring the freehold
interest in the land around the farmhouse when the quarrying arrangement
came to an end, with the last machinery leaving in 1928.

If that is correct, it would explain something which otherwise appears very
difficult to reconcile.

The 1916 agricultural tenancy may have covered both parcels of the farm as
a whole at that time. But if part of that holding subsequently ceased to be
part of the agricultural tenancy because of my family's interest in the
parcel A crystallising into our freehold of parcel A, then the 1938 Western
Ground Rents acquisition and the *1939 revised agricultural tenancy* would
not necessarily concern our farmhouse land. Despite decades of it being
treated as though it did and our occupancy being allegedly permissive,
which is a narrative forced upon us to believe, when it most likely wasn't
the case. And why my nan rejected the premis and my dad too. Until their
dying breaths. I inherit this interest in this land parcel A as heir and
successor.

That is why the 1939 plan was so important and helpful.
The point I would particularly like you to confirm

*When you look at the actual 1939 Western Ground Rents revised tenancy and
its plan, I presume you see the same thing I see?*

My reading is that the plan depicts *Parcel B, the eastern agricultural
land, but does not depict or include Parcel A containing the farmhouse and
the land immediately associated with it.*

If that is what the plan shows, I would be very grateful if you could
simply confirm that.

If I am wrong, I would equally value you telling me that I am wrong and,
ideally, pointing me to the feature of the plan or accompanying document
which demonstrates that.

I am not asking you to determine what that means in law. Only whether *we
are looking at the same physical information in the same historical
document*.

That distinction is crucial because I am increasingly concerned that the
later history may have proceeded on the assumption that there was only one
undivided parcel, when the contemporary records may actually distinguish
two different interests.
I would like to do the same exercise with the other records

Your response itself says:

“With all historical research of this nature, it is necessary to piece
together information from surviving records that have been deposited with
us.”

That is precisely what I am now trying to do.

I understand the scientific process demands you look at the evidence and
tell what it tells. But I've done that, I'm making my case. And I'm
actually drawing the conclusion South Wales might be hexed under a spell
not seeing what I see. We also have hallucination with AI which is why I
ask for this specific clarification of the evidence you hold against my
interpretation of it.

Because in one hand I have the narrative, from court documents and news
articles saying we were squatters. In the other hand I have credible
evidence we had no issue relinquishing their parcel. The problem was all
with us on our parcel. And Western Ground Rents and BP don't appear to ever
had our parcel to be able to assert we were on it permissively. And the
1982 registration of their parcel in their name, is paradoxically based on
an alledged no contest our occupancy was permissive. When its all we've
done since the 40's is challenge it. Almost a century.

I would therefore be grateful if, where reasonably possible, you could look
at the relevant surviving records and tell me whether the documentary
evidence supports, contradicts, or simply does not establish the following:

*1. 1916*

I think the 1916 agricultural tenancy appears to encompass the whole farm
as it then stood. Weather it was 2 seperate parcels then I don't know.

*2. 1877 / 1928*

Do the surviving Thomas/Williams/quarrying records support or contradict
the proposition that the farmhouse parcel was treated differently from the
eastern agricultural land, and that the relevant quarrying arrangement had
an effect on the family's interest in that land by 1928?

*3. 1938*

Does the Western Ground Rents conveyance or associated material show that
WGR acquired the farmhouse/house plot itself, or does it appear to concern
only the agricultural interest which subsequently appears in the 1939
tenancy?

*4. 1939*

Does the revised WGR tenancy plan contain only the eastern agricultural
parcel, excluding the farmhouse and its immediate land?

This is the point on which I would particularly appreciate a direct
confirmation or correction.

*5. 1955 / 1962 / 1974*

Do the surviving records contain any express documentary act which actually
transferred, extinguished or otherwise conclusively disposed of the
family's claimed interest in the farmhouse parcel?

I am deliberately not asking you to determine the legal effect of those
events. I am asking whether such an express documentary act appears in the
records.

*6. Later title history*

Do the surviving Glamorgan Archives records contain documentary evidence
showing how the farmhouse parcel itself passed from the earlier family
interest into Western Ground Rents, BP or another owner before the 1982/83
registration?

Or is that documentary chain simply not present in the surviving archive?
I would genuinely welcome correction

I want to emphasise this because I do not want this correspondence to
become an exercise in asking the Archive to validate my theory.

If I have misunderstood the records, *please tell me plainly*.

If the records support what I am seeing, please tell me that plainly too.

And if the surviving material cannot establish the point either way, that
is also a useful and perfectly acceptable answer.

Something as simple as:

*Supported by the surviving record*
*Not supported / contradicted by the surviving record*
*Cannot be determined from the surviving record*

would be enormously helpful to me, together with the relevant reference
where possible.

I am particularly keen to establish this because the research has already
demonstrated the value of going back to the underlying documents rather
than relying upon later descriptions of them. The 1877 material is a good
example: what initially appeared to be an inconsistency has been capable of
being reconsidered once the underlying research and records were examined.

That has made me realise that I need to make sure that I am not making the
same mistake in reverse.

I do not want to build an elaborate theory around a document which I have
simply misunderstood.
I am not asking the Archive to become a party to the dispute

I completely understand the distinction between an archive holding a record
and a court or Land Registry determining legal title.

I am not asking Glamorgan Archives to adjudicate the dispute, give me legal
advice, determine ownership, or take sides against any present landowner or
public authority.

I am asking for something considerably narrower:

*I want to know whether the historical documentary evidence held by the
Archive actually shows what I think it shows.*

That seems to me to be a legitimate research question for an archive
service, particularly where the answer can be expressed simply by reference
to what is physically depicted or expressly recorded in the documents.

I also appreciate that the statutory FOI duty itself does not necessarily
require an archive to create a new interpretation of information merely
because a requester asks for one. I am not trying to turn this into such a
demand. I am asking for professional assistance and dialogue in
understanding the historical material, which seems consistent with
Glamorgan Archives' own published access principles concerning open two-way
communication, active participation by users and responsiveness to the
community it serves. The wider Archive Service Accreditation framework
likewise recognises access and engagement with communities as a core part
of the function of an archive service.

I think that distinction is important.
Why this matters to me

I am trying to establish what actually happened to my late grandmother and
father's claimed ownership of their home and land.

My family maintained that claim for decades. The claim was contested. The
matter eventually resulted in the loss of possession and the subsequent
demolition of the farmhouse.

I completed 22 years of military service in 2024, leaving my career with
honour. I am now approaching this as a researcher trying to establish the
documentary truth of a family and community history.

I am not asking anyone to believe my family merely because it is our family
history.

Quite the opposite.

*I want the records to decide what can and cannot properly be said.*

That is why I would value an open exchange with the people who hold those
records.

If you look at the 1939 plan and say, “No, Sion, I don't think it excludes
the farmhouse parcel, and this is why,” I would consider that extremely
useful.

If you say, “Yes, I can see exactly what you are seeing — the plan depicts
the eastern agricultural land and does not include the farmhouse parcel,”
that is equally important.

And if the surviving records simply do not allow the point to be
determined, I would rather have that stated clearly than have either of us
infer something which the evidence cannot sustain.

I think that is the most constructive way for us to proceed.

There is a shared interest here in getting the history right. These are
records of the community in which we all live, and I think their greatest
value is realised when the surviving evidence can be examined openly,
critically and collaboratively.

I would therefore be very grateful if you could engage with the question at
that documentary level and tell me, as plainly as possible, *whether you
see what I see*.

Thank you again for all your assistance so far. I genuinely appreciate it.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

copy) for consideration.

Best regards

---
Dr Mo Misra, Chair Llandough Community Council

On 2026-09-21 03:59, Sion Buckler wrote:

> Dr Misra,
>
> Thank you for replying, and for doing so promptly and at a weekend.
> Good drills Sir. What an honour. I know you and the Council serve as
> volunteers, and I am grateful for the time.
>
> Let me set out plainly what I am asking of the Council, which is
> narrow. If you'll allow me?
>
> I am not asking your Council to revisit Mr Egan's answer of 14 June
> 2026. He explained that the minute books from 1982 onwards were
> deposited with Glamorgan Archives in 2002, and I am pursuing those
> there.
>
> What I am asking about is what that answer did not cover. Llandough
> Community Council is a public authority under Schedule 1, Part II,
> paragraph 7(b) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. The Act applies
> to the recorded information set out below generally; the Environmental
> Information Regulations 2004 apply in addition to any part of it that
> is environmental information.
>
> PART ONE -- REQUEST FOR RECORDED INFORMATION
>
> 1. Whether the Council holds any recorded information created after the
> 2002 deposit -- minutes, correspondence, reports, emails, photographs
> or files of any kind -- concerning Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) / Church
> View Close, the village green in front of St Dochdwy's including
> registered green VG 41, or the roadside verge by the churchyard wall.
>
> 2. Whether the Council holds any photographs, postcards or images of
> the farm, the barn, the green or the church surroundings, of any date.
>
> 3. Whether the Council holds any recorded information showing what, if
> anything, transferred to it from Penarth Town Council at the 1982
> reorganisation, and any recorded information identifying where the
> pre-1982 Llandough community records were deposited.
>
> If the answer to any of these is that no such information is held, I
> would be content with a short statement to that effect -- but I do need
> it stated. Section 1(1)(a) of the Act requires the Council to confirm
> or deny whether the information is held.
>
> Section 10 (and regulation 5 of the EIR) allows twenty working days
> from receipt, which on my request of 20 September 2026 I calculate as
> 16 October 2026.
>
> If the Council is refusing, section 17 (and regulation 14) requires a
> written refusal notice identifying the exemption or exception relied
> on; section 17(7) requires the Council to give particulars of any
> complaints procedure it operates, or to state that it has none, and to
> notify me of my right to apply to the Information Commissioner; and
> regulation 11 gives a right to an internal review of any refusal under
> the EIR.
>
> "We have nothing more to add" does not meet those requirements. If the
> period passes without a compliant response I will have no option but to
> complain to the Information Commissioner.
>
> PART TWO -- MATTERS FOR THE COUNCIL'S DISCRETION
>
> These are not part of the request above and carry no deadline. They are
> simply things I would be grateful for.
>
> A. I am not asking for the name or contact details of any individual. I
> am asking whether the Council would be willing to pass my details to
> any former member, former clerk or long-standing resident who might
> remember the village between the 1950s and the 1990s, leaving it
> entirely to them whether to contact me. I appreciate the Council may
> have data protection or administrative reasons for declining, and I
> would not press it.
>
> B. Whether the Council would be willing to table this correspondence at
> a meeting and minute it. I am content for it to be tabled in full.
>
> C. Whether the Council would consider, in due course, whether an
> interpretation board or a plaque near the green would be appropriate.
> The excavation on the land beneath Church View Close recorded 1,026
> burials, described in the published report as by far the largest early
> medieval burial population so far recovered from Wales, above a Roman
> villa and an Iron Age roundhouse. That history belongs to Llandough as
> much as to my family, and there is nothing on the ground that records
> it. I would be glad to give the Council or the community a short talk
> on the documentary record, without charge, if that would be useful.
>
> I should be grateful for a response to items 1 to 3 by 16 October 2026.
>
> Regards,
>
> Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
> Royal Signals Cyber/ Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member
>

> wrote:

>>
>> Thanks for your email of 20th September 2026.
>>
>> I note that our Clerk, Paul Egan, has already directed you to all the
>> information we have on the matter as indicated in paragraph 6 of your
>> email.
>>

>>

thread_title: RC26-0375 - Ty Mawr/ Great House, Llandough, Cardiff
subject: RC26-0375 - Ty Mawr/ Great House, Llandough, Cardiff
note: Reply written in Welsh; summary translation of the reply's own sentences given here, with the English quotation from Archive 6048945 verbatim.
body:
[Translated from Welsh] As stated in my emails of 28 May, 10 June and 11 June, there are no letters or records about this site, Tŷ Mawr Farm, Llandough, in our registered files, the only campaign records we keep long-term. No records have come to light since. The only information we hold about the site, including its demolition, is in our archive, the National Monuments Record of Wales: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/sites/20182/archives. Aerial photograph searches are charged.

The armour found in the late nineteenth century is not mentioned in Richard Suggett's unpublished report, Archive 6048945. Most of that record is reproduced as Heneb's site description GGAT02038s:

‘Great House Farmhouse and barn formed an attractive group, built of local lias limestone, and occupied an historic site next to the parish church. Finds of medieval ironwork and pottery have been reported from the site. Great House was the chief freehold farm of the parish and was occupied by the Vaughan's, a minor gentry family, from the mid C16 until the latter part of the C18. Several memorial inscriptions relating to the family are preserved in the church and churchyard. In the early C19 the freehold was acquired by the Bute Estate and the manorial courts for Llandough and Leckwith were held in Great House.

‘Externally both farmhouse and barn appeared to be of nineteenth-century date. Internally, however, surviving vernacular detail- a blocked stone fireplace stair and ogee-stopped beams- suggested a seventeenth-century date for the house. The ground floor of the house was surveyed in unusual circumstances in 1974 by H.J.T. Much detail was then concealed and it was not possible to examine the first floor and roof trusses. The house remained partially recorded because of problems of access created by an ownership dispute. The house and farm buildings were suddenly and completely demolished by B.P. Properties Ltd. on 6th December 1988 amid considerable local controversy.

‘The plan of Great House was not published in the Inventory of Farmhouses & Cottages because of the incompleteness of the available information but it was classified as a sub-medieval house of direct-entry type (site no. 425). However, certain features suggested that the core of the house may have been medieval. Unfortunately it was not possible to examine the fabric of Great House before the demolition of the house.’

Two records refer to the armour: Archive 6048942 (‘At one time it was reputed to be the stable of a Castle, which could be verified by the finding of the remains of a soldier in armour, his horse, lance and small shield under the dining room floor’) and Archive 6048944, a Daily Telegraph article of 16 April 1974 (‘...the discovery beneath the dining room floor in about 1870 of the remains of a soldier in armour, his horse, a lance and shield’).

Archives 6364275 and 6364276 relate to Tŷ Mawr, Tresimwn (Bonvilston) and 33 Whitecross Street, Monmouth, not Tŷ Mawr, Llandough.

Richard Suggett, a member of our survey team, visited the site briefly after its demolition in December 1988 (Archive 6048945), but the reason for the visit is not recorded. We have no letters or records about the letters between ‘C.N. Johns and Mrs Buckler, Great House Farm’. NA/GL/88/49 is the accession number for Suggett's description (Archive 6048945). The only record received under NA/GL/89/208 was Archive 6048941, which is reproduced in GGAT's 1990 report ‘Land at Great House Farm, Llandough. An Archaeological Assessment’ (Archive 6524751). Further enquiries will be treated as public enquiries and may be charged.

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your email of 21 September 2026 making a request for
information.

We are treating your correspondence as a request for information under
the Freedom of Information Act 2000 (the act).

Under the provisions of the act and as defined by "The Freedom of
Information and Data Protection (Appropriate Limit and Fees) Regulations
2004" (the regulations) , an authority is not obliged to comply with a
request for information if the authority estimates that the cost of
complying with the request would exceed the "appropriate limit". This
appropriate limit is set by the regulations at £450 for our type of
authority.

In the regulations our staff time is valued at £25 per hour. This has
the effect of imposing a time limit of 18 hours of staff time for
activities specified in the regulations.

  The regulations make the following activities by an authority countable
towards the cost limit.

  	* determining whether it holds the information,

  	* locating the information, or a document which may contain the
information,

  	* retrieving the information, or a document which may contain the
information, and

  	* extracting the information from a document containing it.

  We have estimated the time and therefore costs as provided by the
regulations, and in doing so have taken into account the above
activities.

  We estimate that this work will take in excess of 18 hours of effort by
our staff. As we have a significant amount of documents on file from the
period 2002-2016 where minutes are in documents rather than published on
the website or in archives.

  We estimate this will exceed the limit provided for by the regulations
and therefore your request is refused on the grounds provided for under
section 12 of the act.

Our estimate of time is based on the requirement to search all minutes
of the council and its committees for a period of 14 years. It is
estimated that it will take about 20 minutes to read each set of minutes
of which there are estimated to 224 sets of minutes. It is considered
that this is likely to take about 10 minutes to assess each set of
minutes a total of over 2240 minutes which equates to 37 hours.

  We may may be able to provide some information if you are able to
reduce or refine your request to bring the cost of compliance under the
regulations limit. We suggest that you could limit the time frame of
minutes that we would need to look through. For example 2002-2006.

  Please contact us if you would like to refine your request.

  If you are not satisfied with this response or you wish to complain
about any aspect of the handling of your request, then you should
contact us in the first instance and we will undertake an internal
review.

  If after the internal review you wish to complain further then you can
complain to the Information Commissioners Office http://www.ico.gov.uk
[1] and request a decision notice.

The other matters you include in your email will be considered at the
October meeting of the council and I will let you have the views of the
council after the meeting.

  Kind regards,
